mcq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Given } f(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & 0 \leq t \leq 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \text{ and its Fourier transform } F(s) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{\sin(2s)}{s}, \text{ use Parseval's identity to find } \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( \frac{\sin(2s)}{s} \right)^2 ds.\)
\(\text{The convolution of } f(t) = e^{-t}u(t) \text{ with itself, where } u(t) \text{ is the unit step, has a Fourier transform equal to:}\)
\(\text{Using Parseval's identity for Fourier cosine transforms with } f(x)=e^{-x} \text{ and the convolution theorem, if } h(x) = (f * f)(x), \text{ then } \int_0^\infty h(x)^2 dx \text{ equals:}\)

\(\text{For the triangular function } f(x) = \begin{cases} 1-|x|, & |x| \leq 1 \\ 0, & |x| > 1 \end{cases}, \text{ use Parseval's identity and the convolution theorem to find } \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left( \frac{\sin(s/2)}{s} \right)^4 ds.\)

\(\text{Evaluate } \int_0^\infty \frac{dx}{(x^2+1)^4} \text{ using Parseval's identity for Fourier cosine transforms and the fact that the Fourier transform of } e^{-|x|} \text{ is } \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{1}{1+s^2}.\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Take } f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & |x| < 1 \\ 0 & |x| > 1 \end{cases}, \text{ then } F(s) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{\sin s}{s}\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Parseval: } \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |f(x)|^2 dx = 2\)

(1 Mark)

\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |F(s)|^2 ds = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{2}{\pi} \frac{\sin^2 s}{s^2} ds = \frac{4}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\sin^2 s}{s^2} ds\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Equate: } 2 = \frac{4}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\sin^2 s}{s^2} ds\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Hence } \int_{0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2 dx = \frac{\pi}{2}.\)

(1 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Using Parseval's identity for Fourier transform, evaluate } \int_{0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{\sin x}{x}\right)^2 dx.\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Take } f(x)=e^{-x}, g(x)=e^{-2x}, \text{ then } F_c(s) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{1}{1+s^2}, G_c(s) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{2}{4+s^2}\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Parseval for cosine transforms: } \int_{0}^{\infty} f(x)g(x) dx = \int_{0}^{\infty} F_c(s) G_c(s) ds\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{LHS: } \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-3x} dx = \frac{1}{3}\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{RHS: } \int_{0}^{\infty} \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{1}{1+s^2} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{2}{4+s^2} ds = \frac{4}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(1+s^2)(4+s^2)} ds\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Equate: } \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(1+s^2)(4+s^2)} ds\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{Hence } \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(x^2+1)(x^2+4)} = \frac{\pi}{12}.\)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Using convolution theorem and Parseval's identity, evaluate } \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(x^2+1)(x^2+4)}.\)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
Take \(f(x) = e^{-ax}\), then \(F_c(s) = \mathcal{F}_c\{e^{-ax}\} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{a}{a^2 + s^2}\)(3)
Parseval's identity: \(\int_{0}^{\infty} [f(x)]^2 dx = \int_{0}^{\infty} [F_c(s)]^2 ds\)(2)
LHS: \(\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2ax} dx = \frac{1}{2a}\)(2)
RHS: \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \left( \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{a}{a^2 + s^2} \right)^2 ds = \frac{2a^2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{ds}{(a^2 + s^2)^2}\)(3)
Equating: \(\frac{1}{2a} = \frac{2a^2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{ds}{(a^2 + s^2)^2}\)(2)
Thus \(\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{ds}{(a^2 + s^2)^2} = \frac{\pi}{4a^3}\)(3)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Using Parseval's identity for Fourier cosine transform, evaluate } \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{(a^2+x^2)^2}.\)
